title: The Impact of Generative AI on Student Learning Outcomes: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies (2020–2025)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how generative artificial intelligence affects student learning outcomes, engagement, motivation, cognitive development, and academic performance in education, especially higher education. The review responds to rapid adoption of tools such as ChatGPT, Whisper, DALL-E, Bard, Copilot, and related large language model systems, while noting concerns about academic integrity, over-dependence, content accuracy, and institutional readiness.

The approach is a systematic review following the PRISMA framework. The author searched Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed empirical studies published from 2020 to June 2025 that examined generative AI use in educational contexts and reported measurable learning outcomes. After screening 145 records and reviewing 35 full-text articles, 12 empirical studies were included. The reviewed studies used varied designs, including cross-sectional surveys, quasi-experimental studies, mixed-methods research, and design-based evaluation, and examined tools such as ChatGPT/GPT-3.5/GPT-4, DALL-E, Grammarly, Bard, Bing AI, and Whisper.

The reviewed evidence spans multiple countries and regions, including China, Taiwan, India, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, Australia, Uruguay, the United States, Hong Kong, and a global sample of higher education students. Populations included primary school pupils, undergraduate and college students, higher education students, and educators. Most studies focused on higher education, with some attention to elementary/primary schooling and ESL learning contexts.

The review concludes that generative AI can improve student productivity, engagement, motivation, writing support, personalization, access to feedback, and learning efficiency. However, effects on deeper outcomes such as critical thinking and long-term academic performance are more context-dependent. The paper emphasizes that benefits depend on AI literacy, discipline, emotional well-being, and pedagogical design, and argues that institutions need clear ethical policies, educator support, and careful integration to reduce risks related to plagiarism, misinformation, bias, privacy, and over-reliance.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large-language-model product family, including ChatGPT, GPT-3.5, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, and ChatGPT-3.5/4 as normalized to the ChatGPT family.
identified_tools.use_case: The review synthesized empirical studies using ChatGPT for student feedback, academic writing support, lesson personalization, collaborative interdisciplinary learning, assessment-item generation, student learning support, and student or educator perceptions in higher education and primary education.

findings.finding_summary: Across ChatGPT-focused studies in the review, students reported improved learning efficiency, initiative, creativity, writing confidence, and motivation, but effects on measured performance were not consistently demonstrated. Fan et al. (2025) reported that over half of n=148 engineering students said generative AI improved learning efficiency, initiative, and creativity, while performance was unchanged and concerns about accuracy and reliability remained.
findings.measure: self-reported learning efficiency, initiative, creativity, independent thinking, and academic performance

findings.finding_summary: Mahapatra (2024) reported a positive impact of ChatGPT as a feedback tool for undergraduate ESL students. The review states that n=134 students showed improved academic writing quality and confidence and reduced anxiety, but it does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals.
findings.measure: ESL academic writing skills, writing confidence, and anxiety

findings.finding_summary: Zhu et al. (2023) studied ChatGPT with n=130 undergraduate students in collaborative interdisciplinary learning and reported high educational potential, including support for interdisciplinary digital literacy and collaborative learning. The review also notes risks to critical thinking and creativity, the need for multiple prompts, and limitations with complex or nuanced tasks.
findings.measure: collaborative interdisciplinary learning, digital literacy, critical thinking, and creativity

findings.finding_summary: Jauhiainen and Garagorry Guerra (2024) studied ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 with n=110 primary-school students in Uruguayan schools. The review reports that ChatGPT enabled real-time personalization of lessons, enhanced motivation and performance, and aligned content adaptation with curriculum goals and individual learning needs.
findings.measure: lesson personalization, student motivation, and performance

findings.finding_summary: Ravšelj et al. (2025) surveyed n=23,218 higher-education students from 109 countries and territories about ChatGPT. The review reports that about 70% found ChatGPT interesting and that it was helpful for general knowledge and simplifying information, but it was less prominent in enhancing soft skills and was rarely used for creative tasks.
findings.measure: student perceptions of ChatGPT usefulness, interest, use, knowledge support, and soft-skill support

findings.finding_summary: Bhandari et al. (2024) evaluated ChatGPT-generated algebra questions with n=207 test respondents. ChatGPT-generated questions were comparable to textbook items in difficulty and discrimination, with no significant difference reported, and showed strong learning-objective alignment with a similarity score of 0.9666.
findings.measure: psychometric quality of generated assessment questions: difficulty, discrimination, and learning-objective alignment

findings.finding_summary: Johnston et al. (2024) surveyed n=2,555 University of Liverpool students and found high awareness of generative AI tools, with 93% awareness reported. Students supported limited academic uses such as grammar support but resisted full essay writing through ChatGPT and requested clearer university policies; concerns included academic integrity, referencing errors, and possible misrepresentation of content.
findings.measure: student awareness, academic use, acceptable-use perceptions, and policy concerns

findings.finding_summary: Jingwei He et al. (2025) surveyed n=680 students at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and reported high ChatGPT popularity and 82.36% AI-literate students. The review states that the findings supported AI curriculum integration but also raised concerns about academic dishonesty and ChatGPT accuracy and reliability.
findings.measure: AI literacy, ChatGPT use, curriculum-integration support, and academic-integrity concerns

identified_tools.name: DALL-E
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s image-generation product family, referenced in the paper as DALL-E/DALL-E-3 for generating visual or course-related content.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included studies where DALL-E/DALL-E-3 was used as part of generative-AI toolsets for course-content generation and higher-education teaching support.

findings.finding_summary: Banjade et al. (2024) evaluated a generative-AI-powered tutoring-system prototype using DALL-E-3 alongside ChatGPT and Whisper. The review reports that the system helped tutors quickly create and customize course content, supported flexible student learning through text, audio, and chatbots, and saved educator time, while also raising concerns about misreading complex content, privacy, bias, and limited personalization.
findings.measure: prototype evaluation of course-content creation, customization, flexible learning support, and educator time savings

findings.finding_summary: Lee et al. (2024) studied educators’ perspectives on several generative AI tools, including DALL-E, with n=30 survey respondents and n=8 interviewees. The review reports that 48.3% of staff used AI in teaching, fewer used it in administration or research, and concerns about academic integrity and AI accuracy were mixed and ambiguous.
findings.measure: educator use of generative AI in teaching, administration, and research; concerns about integrity and accuracy

identified_tools.name: Whisper
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s automatic speech-recognition product, referenced as Whisper for audio or speech-related support within a generative-AI tutoring system.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included Whisper as part of a multimodal generative-AI tutoring-system prototype supporting audio-based student learning access.

findings.finding_summary: Banjade et al. (2024) evaluated a generative-AI-powered tutoring-system prototype that included Whisper alongside ChatGPT and DALL-E-3. The review reports that the system supported flexible learning through text, audio, and chatbots and helped educators automate lesson-planning tasks, although risks included content misinterpretation, data privacy, bias, and limited personalization.
findings.measure: prototype evaluation of multimodal learning support, including audio-based learning access

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational generative-AI chatbot family; the paper refers to Google Bard, which is normalized to Gemini.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included Google Bard as one of several generative AI tools examined in a study of higher-education educators’ teaching, administrative, and research practices.

findings.finding_summary: Lee et al. (2024) studied higher-education educators’ perspectives on several generative AI tools, including Google Bard, with n=30 survey respondents and n=8 interviewees. The review reports that 48.3% of staff used AI in teaching, 33.3% in administration, and 28.6% in research, while concerns about academic integrity and AI accuracy were present but mixed.
findings.measure: educator use of generative AI in teaching, administration, and research; perceived risks

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-assisted writing and grammar-support product used for grammar, writing, and language feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The review identified Grammarly as an AI-supported grammar and writing tool that students viewed more favorably than full AI-generated essay writing.

findings.finding_summary: Johnston et al. (2024) surveyed n=2,555 University of Liverpool students and found support for grammar tools such as Grammarly. The review contrasts this acceptance with resistance to full essay writing through ChatGPT and notes that students wanted clearer university policies on acceptable generative-AI use.
findings.measure: student acceptance of grammar-support tools and perceptions of acceptable academic AI use

identified_tools.name: Bing AI
identified_tools.description: Microsoft’s Bing AI chatbot product, referenced as one of the generative AI tools examined in educator-perspective research.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included Bing AI as one of multiple generative AI tools considered in a study of higher-education educators’ perspectives on learning and teaching.

findings.finding_summary: Lee et al. (2024) included Bing AI among the generative AI tools discussed by higher-education educators, with n=30 survey respondents and n=8 interviewees. The review reports that 48.3% of staff used AI in teaching, but views were mixed because of concerns about academic integrity and AI accuracy.
findings.measure: educator use of generative AI in teaching and concerns about accuracy and integrity

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools or unspecified AI tools used in education where the reviewed study did not identify a specific named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included at least one study of unspecified AI tools in college learning, focusing on motivation, self-efficacy, and critical-thinking awareness rather than a specific named product.

findings.finding_summary: Jia and Tu (2024) studied unspecified AI tools with n=637 college students and found that AI may boost critical thinking indirectly by improving self-efficacy and learning motivation. The review notes limitations including marginal model fit and weak or non-significant relationships for some paths, so the evidence for direct critical-thinking improvement was limited.
findings.measure: critical thinking awareness, general self-efficacy, learning motivation, and perceived AI capabilities

quality_tier_rationale: This is a PRISMA-style systematic review of 12 empirical studies, but it is a narrative synthesis rather than a meta-analysis. The included evidence is largely cross-sectional, mixed-methods, quasi-experimental, or prototype-based, with many findings based on self-report and no pooled statistical estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally positive but mostly qualitative or self-reported impacts on engagement, productivity, motivation, writing confidence, personalization, and assessment generation. No pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported, and at least one study noted unchanged performance, so the magnitude of impact is unclear.
